solution.concept_anchor: LTCCS institutions — SCARDBs and PCARDBs — two-tier structure
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students know the Vaidyanathan Committee examined LTCCS and may incorrectly pair 'LTCCS revival' with the 2004 committee report — confusing the dates of the two separate Vaidyanathan reports.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): PACS are part of STCCS (short-term working capital), not LTCCS — pairing PACS with LTCCS is an entity-swap error.
Eliminate option (b): The Vaidyanathan Committee's LTCCS report was submitted in 2006, not 2004 — 2004 was the STCCS report. Temporal error makes (b) incorrect.
Eliminate option (c): 'SCBs' (State Cooperative Banks) are the apex of the STCCS three-tier structure, not LTCCS. LTCCS uses SCARDBs at the state level — pairing SCBs with LTCCS is incorrect.

Confirm option (d): State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) and Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) are the two tiers of LTCCS — correctly paired.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) exploits temporal confusion — both Vaidyanathan reports (2004 for STCCS, 2006 for LTCCS) are from the same committee, and students who recall one date may apply it to the wrong report. Option (a) exploits entity confusion — PACS are the most visible cooperative credit institution, and students may incorrectly assume they participate in LTCCS. The correct answer requires knowing the specific institutional names (SCARDB, PCARDB) unique to the LTCCS.
solution.final_explanation:
The Long-Term Cooperative Credit Structure has a distinct institutional architecture different from the more commonly discussed STCCS.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: PACS are the base unit of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (crop loans, working capital). LTCCS institutions for investment credit are SCARDBs and PCARDBs — PACS have no role in LTCCS.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: The Vaidyanathan Committee report on LTCCS revival was submitted in 2006, not 2004. The 2004 report addressed STCCS revival.
• Option (c) — Incorrectly matched: State Cooperative Banks are the apex of STCCS. LTCCS is headed by State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) — different institutions.
• Option (d) — Correctly matched: LTCCS operates through a two-tier structure: SCARDBs at the state level and PCARDBs at the district/primary level. This is the standard institutional description of the LTCCS.

Value Addition:
• LTCCS provides long-term investment credit (5–20 year loans) for land purchase, irrigation, farm mechanisation, and orchard development.
• LTCCS institutions have declined significantly — many SCARDBs and PCARDBs are financially unviable.
• NABARD refinances both LTCCS and STCCS, but the majority of NABARD's cooperative credit flows through the more active STCCS.

solution.concept_anchor: Multistate cooperative banks — Central Registrar vs state registrar jurisdiction

statement_analysis.statement: Multistate cooperative banks are registered under the Multistate Cooperative Societies Act, 2002 and their management and membership are governed by the Central Registrar of Cooperative Societies, not a state registrar.
statement_analysis.reason: Multistate cooperative societies — including multistate cooperative banks — are registered with and governed by the Central Registrar under the MSCS Act, 2002, as they operate across state boundaries.

statement_analysis.statement: While the management and membership of multistate cooperative banks fall under the MSCS Act, their banking operations remain subject to RBI's oversight under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
statement_analysis.reason: The dual regulation framework applies to multistate cooperative banks too — RBI regulates banking operations while the Central Registrar governs cooperative society functions under MSCS Act.

statement_analysis.statement: Following the Supreme Court's ruling in Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021), Part IXB of the Constitution no longer applies to multistate cooperative banks.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court upheld Part IXB's applicability to multistate cooperative societies (including multistate cooperative banks) — it only struck down Part IXB's application to state cooperative societies. Multistate cooperatives remain subject to Part IXB.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB in 2021 may not recall the partial nature of the ruling and mark Statement 3 as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Multistate cooperative banks are registered under MSCS Act, 2002 with the Central Registrar — not state registrar. This is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Dual regulation (RBI for banking, Central Registrar for management) applies to multistate cooperative banks — correct.

Critically examine Statement 3: The Rajendra N. Shah ruling (2021) struck Part IXB only for STATE cooperative societies. It upheld Part IXB for multistate cooperative societies — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a geographic-swap trap — it applies the constitutional ruling's outcome to the wrong category of cooperative society. The Supreme Court's ruling specifically distinguished between state cooperative societies (state subject, Part IXB inapplicable) and multistate cooperative societies (Parliament's domain, Part IXB upheld). Swapping the outcome from state cooperatives to multistate cooperatives is the trap. A student who knows the ruling without remembering its federal nuance will accept Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Multistate cooperative banks sit at the intersection of cooperative society law and banking regulation, with a distinct federal dimension.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Multistate cooperative banks are registered under the MSCS Act, 2002 with the Central Registrar of Cooperative Societies — not with any state registrar, because they operate across state boundaries.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The dual regulation framework applies — RBI oversees banking operations while the Central Registrar handles management, membership, and cooperative governance under the MSCS Act.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in Rajendra N. Shah (2021) maintained Part IXB's applicability to multistate cooperative societies. The partial striking down targeted only the provisions imposed on state cooperative societies (a state subject under Entry 32). Parliament has legislative competence over multistate cooperative societies under Entry 44 of the Union List, so Part IXB stands for them.

Value Addition:
• The 2023 MSCS Amendment strengthened governance for multistate cooperatives through concurrent audit and a Cooperative Election Authority.
• Major multistate cooperative banks include banks operating across multiple states with central registration.
• The Ministry of Cooperation (established 2021) oversees the Central Registrar and multistate cooperative sector policy.

statement_analysis.statement: NABARD conducts inspection of State Cooperative Banks on behalf of RBI under Section 35(6) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the precise statutory provision under which NABARD acts as RBI's delegated supervisory authority for rural cooperative banks.

statement_analysis.statement: NABARD's refinancing function involves providing long-term funds to cooperative banks, which the cooperative banks then on-lend to farmers and rural borrowers.
statement_analysis.reason: NABARD refinances cooperative banks (and RRBs and commercial banks) by providing funds at concessional rates, which are then on-lent to end beneficiaries — this is the core of NABARD's development finance mandate.

statement_analysis.statement: NABARD directly regulates and licenses primary cooperative banks (including PACS) operating in rural areas.
statement_analysis.reason: PACS are not regulated or licensed by NABARD. They are governed by state cooperative society laws and are outside the direct regulatory purview of both NABARD and RBI.

statement_analysis.statement: NABARD provides capital assistance and revival packages for financially weak cooperative banks under the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure recapitalisation framework.
statement_analysis.reason: NABARD plays a key role in administering recapitalisation support for weak SCBs and DCCBs, including implementing the Vaidyanathan Committee-recommended revival packages with conditions attached.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Wait, correct_option is c (Only three). The strong distractor is option d — students who conflate NABARD's broad cooperative credit role with direct regulation of PACS will count Statement 3 as correct and select 'All four'.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Section 35(6) of Banking Regulation Act — NABARD inspects SCBs on behalf of RBI — correct.
Verify Statement 2: NABARD refinances cooperative banks for on-lending to farmers — standard NABARD function — correct.

Test Statement 3: 'NABARD directly regulates and licenses primary cooperative banks (including PACS)' — PACS are outside RBI and NABARD's regulatory purview; they are state-law governed. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 4: NABARD's role in STCCS recapitalisation — administering revival packages for weak cooperative banks — correct. Three of four are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 conflates NABARD's extensive role in rural credit infrastructure with direct regulatory authority over PACS. Students who think of NABARD as the omnibus authority for all rural cooperative credit will accept Statement 3 as correct without recalling the critical exception: PACS are not banks, not regulated by RBI, and not regulated by NABARD. The word 'directly' in Statement 3 is the key — NABARD has indirect influence through refinancing but no direct regulatory authority over PACS.
solution.final_explanation:
NABARD's functions in the cooperative banking sector span supervision, refinancing, and recapitalisation — but these functions do not extend uniformly to all cooperative credit institutions.

| NABARD refinances cooperative banks for on-lending to rural borrowers | Correct |

• The STCCS recapitalisation programme under Vaidyanathan recommendations involved a total package of over ₹13,500 crore with state and central government contributions.

solution.concept_anchor: Legislative timeline: MSCS Act 2002 to 97th Amendment 2011 to SC ruling 2021 to MSCS Amendment 2023
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know the 97th Amendment predates the SC ruling may place it first, forgetting the MSCS Act was enacted nine years before the constitutional amendment.
elimination_logic: Anchor the MSCS Act, 2002 as the earliest event — it predates all constitutional and judicial developments in this sequence.
The 97th Constitutional Amendment was enacted in 2011 — it comes after the MSCS Act and before the Supreme Court ruling.
The Supreme Court ruling in Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India was delivered in 2021 — after the amendment it reviewed.
The Multistate Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 is the most recent event; correct sequence: MSCS Act → 97th Amendment → SC ruling → 2023 Amendment, which is option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets the MSCS Act (2002) vs the 97th Amendment (2011) ordering. Students who associate cooperative society law reform with the 97th Amendment may place the amendment first, forgetting the MSCS Act was enacted nine years earlier for multistate cooperatives. The 2002 Act and 2011 Amendment address different aspects (multistate scope vs constitutional framework), but their temporal sequence is the testable dimension here.
solution.final_explanation:
The legislative and judicial evolution of cooperative society governance spans over two decades.

Correct sequence:
1. Multistate Cooperative Societies Act, 2002: Created the legal framework for cooperative societies operating across state boundaries, with the Central Registrar as the governing authority.
2. 97th Constitutional Amendment, 2011: Inserted Article 19(1)(c) (right to form cooperatives) and Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT), constitutionalising cooperative governance norms.
3. Supreme Court ruling — Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India, 2021: Partially struck down Part IXB — upheld for multistate cooperatives, invalidated for state cooperative societies.
4. Multistate Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023: Updated governance framework for multistate cooperatives — concurrent audit, Cooperative Election Authority, dispute resolution.

Value Addition:
• Each development built on gaps exposed by the previous framework — the 2023 amendment addressed governance gaps the 2002 Act had not resolved.
• The 97th Amendment was passed with the ratification of the required number of state legislatures — making the SC ruling's partial invalidation procedurally significant.
• The Ministry of Cooperation (2021) was established between the SC ruling and the 2023 amendment — reflecting policy priority for cooperative sector reform.

solution.concept_anchor: PSL targets — UCBs 40% ANBC; RRBs vs cooperative banks different obligations

statement_analysis.statement: Urban Cooperative Banks are required to achieve a Priority Sector Lending target of 40% of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit, with sub-targets for agriculture, weaker sections, and micro-enterprises.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI prescribes a 40% PSL target for UCBs (same as domestic scheduled commercial banks), along with applicable sub-targets for agriculture, weaker sections, and other priority segments.

statement_analysis.statement: Regional Rural Banks face the same 40% PSL target as Urban Cooperative Banks and follow identical sub-target allocations for agriculture and weaker sections.
statement_analysis.reason: RRBs have a higher PSL obligation — they are required to direct 75% of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit toward Priority Sector activities, with more stringent sub-targets reflecting their rural mandate. Their PSL framework is not identical to UCBs.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Wait, correct_option is (c). Re-evaluating: Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c). Strong distractor is (a) — students who know both RRBs and UCBs serve underserved segments may assume their PSL targets are identical.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: UCBs have a 40% PSL target with sub-targets for agriculture, weaker sections, and micro-enterprises — this is accurate per RBI guidelines; Statement 1 is correct.

Test Statement 2: RRBs have a 40% PSL target identical to UCBs — this is incorrect. RRBs must direct 75% of ANBC to Priority Sector, reflecting their rural credit mandate. The 40% figure applies to domestic commercial banks and UCBs, not RRBs.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates RRBs and UCBs by assuming both face the same 40% PSL target. This is a high-quality trap because both institutions serve underserved populations and are subject to PSL obligations. The critical difference is magnitude: RRBs face a 75% PSL obligation (the highest among bank categories), while UCBs and commercial banks face 40%. A student who knows PSL applies to both but not the differentiated targets will accept Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Priority Sector Lending obligations are calibrated to each bank category's mandate and risk profile — they are not uniform across all lenders.

• Statement 1 — Correct: UCBs must allocate 40% of ANBC to PSL, with sub-targets for agriculture, weaker sections, and micro-enterprises — mirroring domestic commercial banks' PSL framework.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: RRBs face a significantly higher PSL target of 75% of ANBC — not 40%. RRBs are specifically mandated to serve rural, agricultural, and small-business populations, justifying the higher obligation. Their sub-targets also differ from UCBs.

Value Addition:
• PSL shortfalls must be parked in designated funds (RIDF, NABARD funds) — effectively a penalty for under-achievement.
• Foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches face a 40% PSL target but with different sub-target allocations compared to domestic banks.
• The PSL framework is periodically revised by RBI — the 75% RRB target has been a longstanding feature reflecting RRBs' origin mandate under the RRB Act, 1976.

solution.concept_anchor: NCFDC — RBI in-principle approval as umbrella for UCBs
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because NABARD is the most prominent cooperative credit institution and students may assume it serves as the umbrella for all cooperative banks including UCBs.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): DICGC provides deposit insurance — it is not an umbrella institution providing liquidity support, IT infrastructure, or training.
Eliminate option (b): NABARD serves as the umbrella institution for rural cooperative banks (SCBs, DCCBs) — but not for Urban Cooperative Banks. A separate umbrella body was proposed for UCBs.
Eliminate option (c): RBI is the regulator — it is not constituted as an umbrella service provider for UCBs.

Confirm option (d): The National Cooperative Finance and Development Corporation (NCFDC) received RBI's in-principle approval as the umbrella body specifically for Urban Cooperative Banks — providing liquidity support, IT infrastructure, and training.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes NABARD (which students associate with all cooperative banking) for the NCFDC (the correct UCB umbrella). NABARD does serve as a de facto support institution for rural cooperative banks, but a separate organisation was conceptualised and received in-principle approval for UCBs. Students who know an umbrella exists but not which entity it is will select option (b) — the most institutionally prominent wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
The umbrella organisation concept addresses a practical gap — individual UCBs are too small to independently afford core banking technology, cybersecurity infrastructure, and professional training.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: DICGC is a deposit insurance body, not an umbrella institution providing operational support to UCBs.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: NABARD provides refinancing and supervisory support to rural cooperative banks (SCBs, DCCBs) — a different tier of the cooperative structure. UCBs have a separate proposed umbrella.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: RBI is the regulator of UCBs, not a service-providing umbrella institution.
• Option (d) — Correct: The National Cooperative Finance and Development Corporation (NCFDC) received RBI's in-principle approval as the umbrella body for UCBs — aimed at providing shared liquidity support, IT infrastructure (including core banking solutions), and capacity-building training.

Value Addition:
• The NCFDC concept was first recommended by the N.S. Vishwanathan Expert Committee on UCBs (2019).
• The rationale is similar to the CCDFS (Credit Cooperative Development Fund and Support) concept — pooling resources for shared infrastructure.
• Without a common CBS platform, smaller UCBs struggle to offer digital banking services, limiting their competitiveness and financial inclusion reach.

solution.concept_anchor: PMC Bank crisis as trigger for 2020 Banking Regulation Amendment
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify both A and R as factually true may assume the policy response (R) explains the reform (A) without examining whether R is the direct causal explanation.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 extended RBI's regulatory powers over UCBs, including audit oversight, capital requirements, and the ability to initiate amalgamation without moratorium.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. R states 'UCBs had been operating without any regulatory oversight from RBI prior to 2020.' This is factually incorrect — UCBs were already subject to RBI oversight for their banking operations under the Banking Regulation Act before 2020. The 2020 amendment strengthened and expanded RBI's powers; it did not initiate oversight from zero.
Step 3: Since R is factually incorrect, the answer must be (c): A is correct but R is incorrect.
Confirm: correct_option is (c) — A correct, R incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 is a landmark reform — but it is important to understand what it changed versus what was already in place.

Assertion (A): Correct. The 2020 amendment meaningfully expanded RBI's regulatory authority over UCBs — covering audit oversight, capital adequacy norms, and the power to initiate amalgamation or reconstruction without necessarily placing the bank under moratorium first.

Reason (R): Incorrect. UCBs were not operating without RBI oversight before 2020. RBI already regulated UCBs' banking operations under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 — the Act had applied to cooperative banks since 1966. The 2020 amendment strengthened and extended RBI's powers in specific domains; it did not create oversight from scratch. This distinction is crucial — R overstates the pre-2020 regulatory vacuum.

Conclusion: A is correct, R is incorrect — answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• Banking Regulation Act was extended to cooperative banks in 1966 — RBI has had oversight over cooperative banks' banking functions for decades.
• The 2020 amendment specifically filled gaps in audit authority, capital raising, and amalgamation powers — building on the existing framework.
• The PMC Bank crisis (2019) was the trigger — but the reform was about strengthening existing oversight, not creating it anew.

solution.concept_anchor: SFB conversion eligibility — net worth ₹100 crore, dissolution requirement

statement_analysis.statement: RBI's on-tap Small Finance Bank licensing guidelines (2018) permit Urban Cooperative Banks meeting eligibility criteria to voluntarily convert to Small Finance Banks.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI's 2018 on-tap SFB licensing guidelines explicitly created a voluntary conversion pathway for eligible UCBs — this is the formal route by which Shivalik Mercantile Cooperative Bank converted in 2021.

statement_analysis.statement: The minimum net worth requirement for a UCB seeking to convert to a Small Finance Bank under the on-tap licensing guidelines is ₹100 crore.
statement_analysis.reason: RBI's guidelines stipulate a minimum net worth of ₹100 crore as one of the financial eligibility conditions for UCB-to-SFB conversion.

statement_analysis.statement: Once an Urban Cooperative Bank converts to a Small Finance Bank, it continues to operate under the dual regulatory framework — subject to both RBI and the state registrar of cooperative societies.
statement_analysis.reason: Conversion to an SFB requires dissolution of the cooperative society — the entity reconstitutes as a company. Post-conversion, it operates solely under RBI regulation as a scheduled commercial bank, escaping dual regulation entirely.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know the conversion involves regulatory change may misremember that some cooperative oversight persists even after conversion.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: 2018 on-tap SFB guidelines do permit UCB conversion — Shivalik's 2021 conversion confirms this; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: ₹100 crore minimum net worth is the RBI eligibility condition — Statement 2 is correct.

Test Statement 3: Post-conversion, the cooperative society is dissolved and reconstituted as a company — the state registrar has no jurisdiction over a company. Dual regulation ends at conversion; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a partial-truth mechanism — it is true that UCBs are subject to dual regulation. But applying this to the post-conversion entity is incorrect. Conversion requires dissolving the cooperative society entirely. Once a UCB becomes an SFB (a company), it falls outside cooperative society law jurisdiction. The state registrar has no authority over a company registered under the Companies Act. Students who know the conversion occurs may assume some cooperative oversight persists as a transitional feature — it does not.
solution.final_explanation:
The UCB-to-SFB conversion pathway is designed as a clean structural transformation — not a partial regulatory migration.

• Statement 1 — Correct: RBI's 2018 on-tap SFB licensing guidelines explicitly created the conversion pathway. Eligible UCBs may apply voluntarily — the route is established and has been successfully used.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Minimum net worth of ₹100 crore is a financial eligibility condition. UCBs must also demonstrate satisfactory track record and CRAR compliance.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Post-conversion, the SFB is a company, not a cooperative society. The cooperative society is dissolved in the process. The state registrar of cooperative societies has no jurisdiction over the new entity. Dual regulation ends — the converted SFB operates solely under RBI as a scheduled commercial bank.

Value Addition:
• The SFB conversion pathway gives UCBs access to equity markets, branch expansion without state approval, and a single-regulator environment.
• Member consent under one-member-one-vote is required for dissolution — this practical challenge slows conversion even for financially eligible UCBs.
• Post-2021 Shivalik conversion, several other UCBs have expressed interest in the conversion route — watch for new approvals.

solution.concept_anchor: Regulatory jurisdiction — which authority oversees which cooperative bank tier
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because it correctly pairs NABARD with SCBs but incorrectly assigns RBI's direct supervision to DCCBs rather than UCBs, exploiting the NABARD-RBI overlap.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I item D (PACS): PACS are governed by State Cooperative Societies Acts — matched with '4-State Cooperative Societies Acts (no RBI or NABARD direct regulation)'. This eliminates options where D is paired with RBI or NABARD.
List I item A (UCBs): RBI directly supervises Urban Cooperative Banks — matches '1-Directly supervised by RBI under Banking Regulation Act'. Confirms (a) or (b).
List I item B (SCBs): NABARD inspects on behalf of RBI under Section 35(6) — matches '2-Inspected by NABARD on behalf of RBI under Section 35(6) of Banking Regulation Act'.
List I item C (DCCBs): Also inspected by NABARD — matches '3-Inspected by NABARD on behalf of RBI (same supervisory mechanism as SCBs)'. Correct answer is (a): A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works by placing RBI's direct supervision over DCCBs (option c) rather than over UCBs. Students who know RBI supervises some cooperative banks and NABARD supervises others may not remember that NABARD's mandate covers both SCBs AND DCCBs — not SCBs alone. Option (c) gives the correct SCB pairing but swaps RBI and NABARD for UCBs and DCCBs. Only a student who knows all three pairs precisely will correctly identify option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The division of supervisory jurisdiction across cooperative bank tiers is a foundational concept in understanding India's cooperative banking regulation.

Correct matches:
• A–1: Urban Cooperative Banks are directly supervised by RBI under the Banking Regulation Act — not through NABARD. RBI conducts inspections and issues directions directly.
• B–2: State Cooperative Banks are inspected by NABARD on behalf of RBI under Section 35(6) of the Banking Regulation Act — the statutory delegation mechanism.
• C–3: District Central Cooperative Banks are also inspected by NABARD on behalf of RBI under the same Section 35(6) mechanism — sharing the same supervisory channel as SCBs.
• D–4: PACS are governed by State Cooperative Societies Acts, with neither RBI nor NABARD exercising direct regulatory authority over them.

Value Addition:
• This supervisory architecture creates the 'overlap trap': NABARD supervises rural cooperative banks while RBI supervises urban ones — the reverse of what students might expect given NABARD's rural focus.
• The Section 35(6) delegation does not make NABARD the primary regulator — RBI retains ultimate regulatory authority; NABARD acts on its behalf.
• Post-2020 amendment, RBI's direct powers over UCBs were significantly strengthened in areas of audit, capital, and amalgamation.

solution.final_explanation:
The Kisan Credit Card scheme's effectiveness at the grassroots depends on the last-mile delivery institution's technological readiness — a challenge that PACS has faced acutely.

Applicable principle: The 2022 PACS computerisation scheme, through a Common Accounting System and digital integration, directly addresses the technology gap that prevents PACS-linked cooperative banks from conducting real-time KCC operations.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Cooperative banks have been eligible KCC issuers since the scheme's 1998 launch. The constraint is operational, not regulatory eligibility.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Banking Regulation Amendment Act, 2020 targeted governance and capital powers over UCBs — it did not address the technology deficit at the PACS level.
• Option (c) — Correct: The 2022 PACS computerisation scheme establishes a Common Accounting System across approximately 63,000 PACS, enabling real-time credit tracking, KCC operations, and DBT linkage — directly solving the scenario's technology barrier.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Converting PACS into licensed banks would fundamentally alter their legal character and is not the envisaged policy solution. PACS are designed as cooperative societies, not banks.

Value Addition:
• The Common Accounting System under PACS computerisation will standardise financial reporting — currently PACS use varied, often manual systems with no interoperability.
• The scheme is funded by the central government with state participation — estimated to cost approximately ₹2,516 crore.
• Successful implementation will make PACS effective nodes for multiple government schemes including PM-KISAN, PMFBY, and fertiliser subsidy delivery.
